strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and interesting gap: differentially private estimation of geodesic regression parameters on Riemannian manifolds, extending the KNG mechanism (Reimherr & Awan 2019; Soto et al. 2022) beyond the Fréchet mean.

The idea of connecting the sensitivity of the regression parameters to Jacobi fields, and hence to curvature, is elegant and naturally continues the line of work by Reimherr et al. (2021); the Euclidean case recovering private linear regression with sensitivity 2τ/n is a clean corollary.

Appendix B contains a useful empirical validity check: over 100 pairs of adjacent datasets, the ratios of theoretical to experimental sensitivities are always above one, providing evidence that the bounds hold (at least on the constant-curvature sphere).
The manuscript is honest about open problems (efficient samplers for KNG on manifolds, extension to Kendall shape space), and the background material on Riemannian geometry is self-contained.
weaknesses: The central global sensitivity result (Theorem 3.4) appears to apply the Rauch comparison theorem in the wrong direction. Theorem 2.1 states that if K(γ) ≤ K̃(γ̃) then ||J̃|| ≤ ||J||. With Assumption 3.1 (κ ≤ K_max) and M̃ of constant curvature K_max, this yields ||J̃|| ≤ ||J||, i.e., the Jacobi field on the data manifold is *at least as large* as the comparison field, so Δ_p ≤ (2τ/n)||J̃(1)|| does not follow. On the constant-curvature sphere the bound holds trivially (which is what Appendix B empirically confirms), but for manifolds with curvature strictly below K_max, or negatively curved spaces (where Jacobi fields grow and the paper claims generality), the stated global bound appears invalid. As written, the main theoretical claim is unsupported outside constant curvature.

The privacy guarantee of the implemented mechanism is compromised by a data-dependent τ. In Appendix A the sampler replaces τ with max_i ||ε_i||, the empirical maximum error computed from the data, in the acceptance probability. This makes the target density data-dependent in a non-DP-sanctioned way, breaking the claimed pure-DP guarantee of the released (p̃, ṽ). A public (or privately released) bound on residuals would be needed; this is never addressed. It is also unclear whether τ in Assumption 3.2 is a public constant or a data quantity, which matters crucially for the sensitivity calculation itself.

The proofs contain gaps: in Lemma 3.3, equation (14) replaces a sum of two terms involving dpExp(p, x_n v) and dpExp(p, x'_n v) with a single term 2τ||dpExp(p, x'_n v)|| without justification (it requires an unjustified ordering of the derivative norms); in Theorem D.1 the maximization implicitly sets x_n = x'_n = 1 while x ∈ (0,1), and the data-dependent scaling of x to (0,1) is not discussed from a privacy standpoint (data-dependent scaling parameters would leak information).

The experiments are very small in scale and the comparisons are weak. The sphere experiments use n = 20 synthetic points with a single privacy budget; the linear regression comparison uses only 100 rows of the Wine dataset, and the 'outperforms IBM Diffprivlib by approximately 85 times' claim rests on a single small run. Comparing against Opacus DP-SGD—a deep-learning optimizer applied to a two-parameter linear model—is an apples-to-oranges baseline. No real manifold-valued data (e.g., directional data, diffusion tensors, shapes) is evaluated, despite the motivation citing medical imaging and computer vision.

There is a possible inconsistency with the KNG mechanism of Soto et al. (2022): when the normalizing constant depends on the footpoint, the required noise scale is σ = 2Δ/ε, but the sampler in Appendix A uses σ = Δ_p/ε without verifying the normalizing-constant condition on the sphere.

Presentation quality is below the bar: frequent typos ('Riemmanian', 'in D we consider' instead of a reference, 'J̃_p' where J̃_v is meant, wrong equation cross-references such as 'as in 3' in Appendix A), confusing notation in equations (12)–(13) around the unit-vector convention ε̂_n, and Figure 2 reporting a mean angle of 0.10° with standard deviation 5.47° without clarifying the skew. The discussion claims demonstration 'over a variety of sample sizes' but only 11 replicates up to n ≈ 35 are shown (Figure 6).

No code or implementation details sufficient for reproduction are provided (the proposal scale is only specified as η ∝ σ), and no convergence analysis of the Metropolis-Hastings sampler to the KNG target is given, which is required for the DP claim of the released samples.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: differentially private geodesic regression on Riemannian manifolds, connecting parameter sensitivity to Jacobi fields and curvature, which is a natural and potentially useful line of inquiry building on Reimherr et al. (2021) and Soto et al. (2022).

The writing of the geometric background (Section 2, Appendix C) is pedagogically clear, and the idea of exploiting Rauch comparison to convert data-dependent Jacobi-field sensitivities into global bounds is a sensible strategy.
Appendix B makes an effort to empirically validate the sensitivity bounds by comparing theoretical and experimental sensitivities on adjacent datasets, which is good practice in principle.
The framing of linear regression as a special case allows sanity-checking the framework against established DP libraries.
weaknesses: Central soundness gap in the sensitivity analysis: the KNG mechanism requires the sensitivity of the gradient to be bounded at every possible released point z, i.e., a bound on sup_{D~D'} ||∇E(z;D) − ∇E(z;D')|| for all z in the mechanism's support. Lemma 3.3 and Theorem D.1 only bound the gradient difference at the (data-dependent) optimum, where geodesics are τ-close and away from the cut locus. A sample from the KNG density can land anywhere on the manifold, so the claimed pure-DP guarantee is not established as stated.

Circularity and privacy leak in the bound itself: the sensitivity of the footpoint is derived 'for a fixed shooting vector v', but v is itself estimated from the data; the paper never establishes that sanitizing (p, v) jointly with composition ε+ε is valid. Worse, τ is defined as a data-dependent bound on residuals, and Appendix A explicitly replaces τ with the empirical max error max||ϵ_i|| in the acceptance probability — using a data-dependent quantity computed from the raw data without sanitizing it violates DP (or at minimum requires this dependency to be accounted for, which the paper does not do).

The derivation also appears to assume x_n = x'_n = 1 when maximizing (Theorem D.1), effectively requiring bounded, unit-scaled predictors; this scaling assumption is stated only in passing in Section 2.2 and its privacy implications are not discussed.

Experiments are far too weak to support the claims: the manifold case uses a single synthetic dataset of 20 points on S², and the linear-regression comparison uses only the first 100 rows of the Wine dataset with 4 features. There is no varying of ε, n, or noise level systematically in the main text, no confidence intervals for the headline comparison, and no real manifold-valued data (e.g., directional wind or shape data), despite motivating medical imaging and computer vision.

The headline claim that DPGR 'outperforms IBM Diffprivlib by approximately 85 times' is almost certainly an artifact of misconfigured baselines (e.g., unnormalized features or incorrect bounds in Diffprivlib). An MSE of 7.856 against ~0.9 for all other methods, with no tuning details, does not constitute a fair state-of-the-art comparison.

Notation and derivations contain errors that undermine confidence: Appendix A writes the footpoint gradient as ||−(1/n)Σ d²(Exp(p,x_i v),y_i)|| which is dimensionally inconsistent with Equation (5); the claimed Jacobi norms (cos(1), sin(1)) and the statement that positive curvature here *shrinks* sensitivity appear inconsistent with the curvature-inflation phenomenon the paper cites as motivation.

Reproducibility is poor: no code is released or described in detail, the MCMC tuning parameter η is only specified as 'proportional to σ', the number of samples m is not given for Figure 2/3, and the experimental protocol for the baseline libraries is not documented.

Presentation issues: multiple typos ('Riemmanian', 'quanitify', 'data depended'), an unfinished editorial artifact ('in D we consider the sensitivity of the shooting vector' in Section 3), and proof steps justified informally ('the adjoint operator can be thought of as an inner product...').

The conceptual novelty is limited: the core observation that DP sensitivity on manifolds is governed by curvature was already established by Reimherr et al. (2021) and Soto et al. (2022) for the Fréchet mean, as the authors themselves concede; extending this to geodesic regression via a two-parameter decomposition is an incremental step, and the empirical demonstration does not yet establish that this step is reliable enough for others to build on.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely novel and well-motivated problem: releasing differentially private parameters of geodesic regression, which extends the DP-on-manifolds line of work (Reimherr et al. 2021; Soto et al. 2022) from Fréchet means to regression parameters.

The main theoretical idea is elegant: the sensitivity of the footpoint and shooting vector is bounded via Jacobi fields (Lemma 3.3, Theorem 3.4, Theorem D.1), connecting privacy noise calibration directly to curvature through the Rauch comparison theorem. This is a natural but non-trivial extension, and the closed-form solutions on the sphere (||Jp(1)|| = cos 1, ||Jv(1)|| = sin 1) are a nice concrete instantiation.

Appendix B provides an empirical check of the sensitivity bounds via ratios of theoretical to experimental sensitivity over 100 pairs of adjacent datasets, all ratios exceeding one, which supports the validity of the bounds.
The derivation of DP linear regression as a special case (Euclidean manifold) and the comparison against IBM Diffprivlib and Opacus gives at least some grounding in existing tooling.
weaknesses: Potentially serious privacy soundness issue: in Appendix A the sampler replaces the privacy parameter τ with the data-dependent empirical maximum error max||ϵi|| in the acceptance probability. This changes the sampled distribution away from the DP-calibrated KNG mechanism, and no argument is given that the resulting MCMC procedure still satisfies (even approximately) pure DP. Since the DP guarantee is the paper's central claim, this needs to be addressed head-on.

The evaluation is very thin. The sphere experiment uses only 20 synthetic data points with Gaussian noise and projection; the real-data experiment (Wine Quality) uses only the first 100 rows and simple single-feature regression. No real manifold-valued data (medical imaging, shape statistics, directional data) is used despite these domains motivating the paper. Claims of generality to arbitrary Riemannian manifolds, Kendall shape space, etc., remain untested.

The baseline comparison is weak and possibly misleading: the 'outperforms IBM Diffprivlib by approximately 85 times' claim rests on a single dataset, a single ε, no repetitions or error bars, and no evidence the Diffprivlib baseline was properly configured (e.g., data bounds/privacy budget settings that Diffprivlib requires). Opacus DP-SGD is arguably not a like-for-like baseline for private OLS.

Key practical questions are unresolved: how is τ (the τ-closeness assumption 3.2) determined in practice, since the global sensitivity depends on it? How is the MCMC tuning parameter η chosen, and does the chain mix well enough for the reported histograms to reflect the actual mechanism? Details such as m, η, and convergence diagnostics are missing, which harms reproducibility (no code is mentioned).

Several technical details are under-specified or imprecise: the adjoint/parallel-transport manipulations in equations (12)–(13) and (29)–(30) are described informally rather than proven; the maximization arguments ('errors face in opposite directions') are asserted rather than shown; Assumption 3.2's radius bound π/(8√κ) is introduced without derivation; the notation in Lemma 3.3 and the Jp(0) initial conditions is confusing.

Presentation issues throughout: typos ('Riemmanian', 'defacto', 'corroborates recent findings'), a cross-reference bug ('in D we consider the sensitivity of the shooting vector'), the KNG density in Eqn. (10) is missing the norm exponent, the MAE definition in Section 4.1 is actually a mean geodesic distance and its relationship to the energy E is muddled, and Figure 3 reports 'Std Dev 0.00', suggesting reporting precision issues.

Significance is limited by the narrow scope of the results: only the sphere and Euclidean space are worked out; for other manifolds the paper only gestures at 'requires an understanding of the Jacobi fields'. The Euclidean results, meanwhile, largely re-derive known private linear regression with a bound of 2τ/n that does not obviously improve on prior dedicated methods.

The Discussion claims demonstration 'over a variety of sample sizes', but the main text uses n = 20; the sample-size study (Figure 6) uses only 11 replicates due to computational cost, which also casts doubt on the practicality of the MCMC-based sampler.

strengths: First formal treatment of differentially private geodesic regression; the paper plausibly fills a genuine gap, as the authors convincingly argue that existing manifold DP tools (Laplace/Gaussian output perturbation, exponential mechanism, DP-SGD) do not directly transfer to this setting because sensitivities of parameters in different tangent spaces or of the energy itself are nontrivial to bound.

The core theoretical contribution is elegant and geometrically meaningful: the sensitivity of the footpoint and shooting vector is characterized through Jacobi fields and bounded via the Rauch comparison theorem, cleanly extending the curvature-dependent sensitivity phenomena known for the Fréchet mean (Reimherr et al., 2021) to regression parameters.

The empirical validation of the sensitivity bounds (Appendix G) is a nice touch: ratios of theoretical to experimental sensitivity computed over many adjacent-dataset pairs are consistently ≥ 1 and close to 1, supporting both validity and tightness of the bounds.

Demonstrations span three manifolds of practical interest (sphere, Kendall shape space via real ADNI corpus callosum data, SPD(2)), with sensitivity constants instantiated for each, and the appendix derives the full shooting-vector bound and gradient proofs.

The limitations discussion is unusually candid and technically substantive: the data-driven choice of τ, the approximate-DP implications of Metropolis–Hastings sampling, and the difficulty of baselines are all openly analyzed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The implementation does not satisfy the DP guarantee the theory provides: τ is set to max_i ||ε_i||, which is data-dependent, and this non-private quantity is used in the acceptance probability. The authors acknowledge this ('indeed violates privacy'), but the experimental results therefore do not demonstrate a working DP pipeline; no experiment uses a public/conservative τ to show utility under the actually-private mechanism.

Privacy is further weakened by the MCMC sampler (Metropolis–Hastings gives approximate DP with δ = O(1/M)); the claim that M can be set 'arbitrarily large' to make δ negligible is asserted but never instantiated with a concrete chain length, mixing diagnostic, or δ value.

The sequential release procedure has a subtle soundness gap: sensitivity for the footpoint is derived 'for a fixed shooting vector v', but in the KNG sampling procedure the role of v during the footpoint release (and its potential data dependence, e.g., via parallel transport of v̂) is not fully pinned down. The fiber-bundle argument addresses the geometry of sampling but not the data-dependence of the fixed vector.

Experimental evaluation is weak: the utility metric is training-set energy rather than held-out prediction error; there are no baselines or ablations beyond budget-allocation sweeps; and the procedure of generating m² candidate pairs and reporting averages is an unusual protocol — the practically relevant question (how to select one pair within budget, or how utility degrades for a single released pair) is not directly measured.

Internal inconsistencies suggest insufficient polish: the notation for private vs. non-private estimates is swapped in Section 4 relative to earlier sections; the bound stated in Theorem D.1 (page 15) differs from the bound actually derived in the proof (equation 44); and the definition of ∆_v in Appendix G writes ∇_vE(v; D) with a stray argument.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned; the pipeline depends on untracked choices (MCMC tuning η, initialization, number of candidates m), and no statement about availability of the ADNI processing pipeline or code is given.

Assumption 3.2 requires the fit to be τ-close and the data bounded in a geodesic ball with a known radius, assumptions that are hard to verify a priori in practice; the paper does not quantify how sensitive the utility results are to misspecification of these quantities.

strengths: First, natural contribution: the paper appears to be the first to give a differentially private method for geodesic regression on Riemannian manifolds, filling a genuine gap between DP linear regression and DP statistics on manifolds (Fréchet mean, private PCA, etc.).

The sensitivity analysis is conceptually appealing: bounds are derived via Jacobi field equations and the Rauch comparison theorem, cleanly tying the noise scale to the curvature of the manifold (Theorems 3.3 and D.1), which corroborates and extends the curvature-dependent sensitivity phenomena observed for the Fréchet mean (Reimherr et al., 2021).

The sequential footpoint/shooting vector treatment via the fiber-bundle structure of TM is handled carefully, avoiding a spurious global product decomposition, and the composition argument is stated correctly.

Empirical validation of the theoretical bounds (Appendix G, Figures 9–10) with ratios close to 1 across sample sizes on the sphere and SPD(2) is a nice touch that supports tightness of the derived sensitivities.

The limitations discussion is candid: the authors explicitly acknowledge that using max_i ||ε_i|| as τ violates privacy, that Metropolis–Hastings only yields approximate DP (δ = O(1/M)), and that no valid baseline comparisons currently exist for this problem.
weaknesses: The central practical privacy guarantee is undermined. The sensitivity bound requires τ = sup_i d(y_i, Exp(p̂, x_i v̂)), which is data-dependent; the implementation (Appendix A) uses max_i ||ε_i|| computed from the data, which the authors admit 'violates privacy.' The proposed remedy (asking domain experts to pre-specify τ) is speculative and leaves the actual deployed mechanism without a clean DP guarantee. Combined with the approximate MCMC sampler (only approximate-DP), the end-to-end privacy story is considerably weaker than the abstract suggests.

The theoretical contribution, while correct-looking, is a fairly direct composition of existing tools: the manifold KNG mechanism (Soto et al., 2022), the Rauch comparison theorem, and classical Jacobi field computations. The proofs are short chains of triangle inequality + operator norm bounds; for an ICML main-track paper the novelty of the analysis is modest.

The empirical evaluation is thin and largely confirms the obvious: error decreases with larger budget and larger n, and misallocated budgets hurt. Experiments are mostly synthetic with very small noise (δ = 0.001); the real-data (ADNI corpus callosum) evaluation is purely qualitative (visual comparison in Figure 3) with no quantitative utility metrics, no comparison to non-private baselines' statistical behavior, and no downstream task evaluation.

No baselines at all are compared. The discussion explains why existing manifold-DP methods are awkward to apply, but this is asserted rather than demonstrated; even a naive ambient-space Laplace mechanism or projected Euclidean regression would calibrate the reported utility gains.

Inconsistencies that hurt confidence in the presentation: Theorem D.1 in Appendix D states a shooting-vector bound with sinh(√(−κ_l τ))/√(−κ_l), while the boxed equation (44) (and equation (20) in the main text) has sinh(2√(−κ_l(τ_m+τ)))/√(−κ_l(τ_m+τ)); the proof of D.1 also writes ε_n = Log(Exp(p, x_n v), ŷ_n) with an inconsistent symbol. Notation reuses ε for both error vectors and privacy budgets (acknowledged but confusing), and the bound 'r ≤ π/(8√κ_h)' in Assumption 3.2 is not justified in the text.

Applicability constraints are significant: the method assumes data in a geodesically convex ball with known curvature bounds, a τ-close fit excluding the cut locus, and curvature bounded below/above — assumptions that are hard to verify for the motivating domains (medical imaging, computer vision). The paper does not demonstrate a realistic workflow in which these quantities are available publicly.

Reproducibility is limited: the non-private estimates come from an external GitHub snippet (Regmi, 2020), the MCMC tuning (η ∝ σ) is loosely specified, no code release is mentioned, and experimental details (e.g., how many MCMC steps M, burn-in, acceptance rates) are absent.

The writing has an overlong geometry background section (much of Section 2 and Appendices B.1/B.2 is textbook material from Do Carmo/Nakahara) while core methodological details — the actual sampling procedure's privacy accounting and the choice of budget allocation in practice — receive comparatively less rigor.

strengths: Novel and meaningful problem: the paper appears to be the first to address differentially private parameter release for geodesic regression on Riemannian manifolds, filling a genuine gap between the DP-on-manifolds literature (Reimherr et al. 2021; Soto et al. 2022) and manifold-valued regression (Fletcher 2011).

The central theoretical contribution is elegant: sensitivity bounds for both the footpoint and shooting vector are derived via Jacobi field equations and the Rauch comparison theorem, making explicit how privacy cost is governed by manifold curvature. This cleanly extends and corroborates the curvature-sensitivity findings for the Fréchet mean.

The fiber-bundle argument for sequential sanitization of (p, v) is carefully handled — the authors explicitly note the approach does not rely on a global product decomposition TM ≅ M × R^n, which is a subtle point often glossed over.

Empirical validation is more thorough than typical: besides utility experiments on the sphere, SPD(2), and real corpus callosum shape data, Appendix G empirically checks the tightness of the theoretical sensitivity bounds against experimental sensitivities on adjacent datasets, finding ratios concentrated near one.

The limitations discussion is unusually candid: the data-driven choice of τ, the approximate-DP nature of Metropolis–Hastings sampling (δ = O(1/M)), and the absence of baseline methods are all openly acknowledged rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The practical privacy guarantee is compromised in all experiments: the authors set τ = max_i ∥ε_i∥, which is data-dependent, and admit this 'indeed violates privacy.' Since τ directly calibrates the noise scale (σ = 2τ/nε), the mechanism as actually run is not differentially private. While a public upper bound on τ is a plausible fix, none is instantiated, and no privacy-amp experiments (e.g., with a conservative public τ) are provided. This is a material gap between the theoretical claim and the demonstrated system.

The sensitivity analysis has a structural gap regarding the interaction of the two parameters. Theorem 3.3 bounds ∆p 'for a fixed shooting vector v' and Theorem D.1 bounds ∆v for a fixed footpoint, but adjacent datasets induce different optimizers (p̂, v̂) and (p̂', v̂'), and the gradient difference in eq. (10) is not fully specified with respect to which evaluation point z it is taken. The cancellation argument in the proof assumes gradients evaluated at a common parameter, which needs more careful justification when the released optimum itself changes with the data and when p changes the fiber TpM in which v lives.

Evaluation is limited and somewhat self-referential: utility is measured only via the training energy E(p, v; D), the very objective the released geodesic is designed to fit, with no held-out data, no predictive evaluation beyond qualitative shape plots (Figures 3, 8), and no baseline mechanisms (the discussion dismisses output perturbation, objective perturbation, and DP-SGD without empirical comparison). A modest synthetic-data benchmark even against a naive projected-Laplace baseline would substantially strengthen the empirical case.

Sampling raises practical concerns: Riemannian MH yields only approximate DP and the chain-length-dependent δ is not quantified in the experiments; moreover, the experiments generate 100 private (p̃, ṽ) pairs and aggregate, whereas in practice one pair would be released — the utility of a single draw (e.g., variance of E over draws) is not reported.

Assumptions are restrictive: bounded data in a geodesically convex ball with r ≤ π/(8√κh), τ-closeness of the fit, and known curvature lower bounds. These are standard in the manifold-DP literature, but they limit applicability to the advertised domains (medical imaging, computer vision), and the paper does not discuss how one would obtain these constants privately or publicly in practice.

Reproducibility is questionable: the non-private estimates rely on a single GitHub function file (Regmi, 2020), no code release for the DP pipeline or samplers is mentioned, and there are typographical/notation issues (e.g., 'Riemmanian', η ∝ σ without a constant, inconsistent ε/ε usage, dangling reference 'as in 3', garbled Figure 2 caption) that suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

Significance is real but specialized: the contribution is confined to a single-predictor geodesic regression model with the KNG mechanism; multi-predictor and higher-dimensional extensions are left as future work, which narrows the immediate audience.
